cycles.en_text_before_rewrite:
# I Thought It Was an AI Call—But There Was a Person Inside? Meta’s Unexpected Muse Test

Ring, ring... A call came from an AI agent. That was what it seemed. But while the conversation continued, the voice on the other end was not AI. It was a person.

Meta had run a test that produced exactly this kind of surprise.

The setting was the phone feature of Muse, an AI agent. In some calls made through Muse, trained contract workers, not AI, made the calls and carried the conversations through to the end.

It was like an AI costume: take it off, and a person steps out. Of course, having a person handle a call is not automatically bad. A person can take over when AI alone has trouble. As a system, that may even seem useful.

But then a problem appeared.

### What Callers Were Not Told

When contract workers handled calls, sensitive user information could be shared with call-center staff. People feel differently when they think they are speaking to a machine and when they know a person is listening. Names, plans, and private matters are easier to share when you know who is hearing them. The test began without explaining that contract staff might call.

This was where the story changed.

### The Reveal Behind the AI Sign

The reveal was not AI learning to sound human. A human was behind the AI sign. As AI makes calls and reservations, useful features make people want to know whether AI or a person is on the other end. A Meta executive called the undisclosed test a “mistake,” and the “human concierge” feature was rolled back for now.

## In one line

In the AI age, making a voice sound human is not enough: people must first be told who is on the other end.

deviations.claim_in_article: Meta had run a test that produced exactly this kind of surprise.
deviations.issue: This turns the source’s illustrative framing—that the test evoked this scenario—into a claim that the test actually produced this exact surprise, including a person being mistaken for AI. The Ledger confirms that humans handled some calls, but not that a caller experienced this surprise.
deviations.explanation: The wording makes an unverified caller experience definite; the nearby hedge only qualifies what the call seemed to be, not whether the test produced the surprise.
same_fact_id_locations: Opening paragraphs: “A call came from an AI agent… the voice on the other end was not AI. It was a person.”

deviations.claim_in_article: People feel differently when they think they are speaking to a machine and when they know a person is listening.
deviations.issue: This generalizes a psychological response to people broadly. The Ledger records Meta employees’ privacy concerns about possible sharing of sensitive information, not a general finding about how people feel.
deviations.explanation: The article extends a reported employee privacy concern into a general claim about people’s feelings.
same_fact_id_locations: What Callers Were Not Told: “When contract workers handled calls, sensitive user information could be shared with call-center staff.”
What Callers Were Not Told: “People feel differently when they think they are speaking to a machine and when they know a person is listening.”

deviations.claim_in_article: Names, plans, and private matters are easier to share when you know who is hearing them.
deviations.issue: The source says that knowing who is listening matters; this wording adds the causal claim that knowing the listener makes sharing these matters easier. That effect is not in the Ledger.
deviations.explanation: It changes the source’s statement about the importance of listener identity into an unverified cause-and-effect claim about disclosure.
same_fact_id_locations: What Callers Were Not Told: “Names, plans, and private matters are easier to share when you know who is hearing them.”

deviations.claim_in_article: As AI makes calls and reservations, useful features make people want to know whether AI or a person is on the other end.
deviations.issue: This extends from Muse’s phone feature to AI generally and asserts a general effect on what people want to know. The Ledger supports specific Muse calling capabilities, not this broader claim about AI or people’s preferences.
deviations.explanation: The claim generalizes beyond Muse and adds an unverified claim about people’s preferences.
same_fact_id_locations: The Reveal Behind the AI Sign: “As AI makes calls and reservations, useful features make people want to know whether AI or a person is on the other end.”
